lead: Cloud computing did not arrive in one step. It is the commercial end of a long habit: pool many computers so one big job can use them all, and charge each user for the share they take. Three earlier forms of that habit — cluster, grid and utility computing — each solved one part. Clusters pooled machines inside one room. Grids pooled them across organisations. Utility computing put a meter on the pool. Today the same machinery runs a ticket-booking site, a film studio's rendering farm and a bank's overnight batch jobs.

blocks.text: One computer has a ceiling: its memory and cores are fixed, so a job needing more will never finish, however long you wait. The fix is to join many machines with a network and let one job spread across them. The joined machines form a pool, and the network is the pool's weakest link.

The first pooling was time-sharing on a mainframe. One large machine ran many programs while users at cheap terminals took turns. Each user felt they had a private computer, and the costly mainframe never sat idle while someone typed. The habit of charging for a share rather than a machine started here.
In the 1980s and 1990s, cheap personal computers and fast office networks allowed a second version: buy many ordinary machines instead of one expensive one, and join them. That is a cluster.

Three words recur. Homogeneous: the machines are of the same kind. Heterogeneous: they differ in processor, speed or operating system. Middleware: software that sits between the application and the machines and hides their differences.

sections.h3: Cluster computing: one owner, one room

blocks.text: A cluster is a group of similar computers in one place, joined by a fast local network, owned by one organisation and run by one administrator, with software that makes the group look like a single large computer. One machine in it is a node.

A cluster needs a manager. The head node accepts the job, cuts it into parts, sends each part to a worker node and collects the results. Because every node has the same hardware and operating system, the head node can predict how long a part takes and place it fairly.

The network is a LAN, a local area network: fast, cheap and private. Each node keeps its own memory. Pieces of the same job exchange data by passing messages over the LAN, which is fast enough for them to work together while they run. Some clusters add special interconnects that allow one node to reach another node's memory directly, but a plain LAN does not.

Overnight batch runs, such as a bank clearing its transactions.

blocks.text: The limit is fixed size. A cluster is bought, not rented. Its capacity is whatever was installed, and it idles once the big job finishes.

A cluster stops at the edge of its owner's budget. A grid goes past it: it joins machines of different kinds, in different organisations and cities, so a job can use capacity that would otherwise sit idle.

No single administrator runs a grid, so nothing can be assumed. Machines are heterogeneous, logins differ, and each owner has rules about who may use what. Middleware handles this: it signs a user in once, finds machines that user may use, and hides differences in hardware and operating system.

Users are grouped into a virtual organisation (VO): people from several institutions given access to a shared set of machines by agreement. Membership comes from the agreement, not from who employs you.

The resource broker is the middleware part that matches. It reads the job's needs — cores, memory, disk, time — compares them with machines on offer, and decides where each piece runs. Globus-style toolkits are the classic middleware here; only a few universities teach that layer.

The cost is distance. Sites in different cities talk over a WAN, a wide area network, which is slower and less predictable than a LAN. Sharing also means trusting other owners' machines with your data.

Utility computing means selling computing the way an electricity board sells power: you do not buy the generator, you pay for the units you consume. The provider owns the machines and records your use.

The record is a meter. Common metered quantities are server-hours (one server switched on for one hour), gigabytes stored per month, and gigabytes transferred. The bill adds quantity × rate for each item.

Billing alone is not a cloud. Two more pieces are needed. Self-service: you order capacity from a web console, with no e-mail to a salesperson. Elasticity: capacity grows when load grows and shrinks when load falls, so the meter never runs on machines nobody needs. A cloud is utility billing plus self-service plus elasticity on shared hardware; chapter 1.6 shows what exactly is rented.

The order is this. Mainframe time-sharing pooled one machine. Clusters pooled many machines for one owner. Grids pooled many owners' machines. Utility computing put a meter on the pool. The cloud added a self-service switch and automatic scaling. Each stage kept what the one before it built. This is the order in which the ideas build on each other, not a strict timeline: metered charging was talked about in the mainframe years, and grids came later as a way to reach capacity outside one owner's walls.

examples.question: A ticket-booking site needs 300 servers for 5 working days each month, and 20 servers for the other 20 working days. One server costs ₹80,000 to buy, and running 300 servers costs ₹3,00,000 per month in power, cooling and staff. Renting costs ₹30 per server-hour, charged only for servers that are switched on. Compare the two options over the first 12 months and state the saving from renting.
steps: Peak server-hours per month = 300 servers × 5 days × 24 hours = 36,000 server-hours.
Off-peak server-hours per month = 20 servers × 20 days × 24 hours = 9,600 server-hours.
Total billed server-hours per month = 36,000 + 9,600 = 45,600 server-hours.
The ₹30 per server-hour rent is taken to include power, cooling and staff, so the rented side carries no separate running cost; the bought side pays ₹3,00,000 per month on top of the purchase price.
examples.answer: Renting costs ₹1,64,16,000 over 12 months and buying costs ₹2,76,00,000, so renting saves ₹1,11,84,000 because the bought servers sit idle for 20 of the 25 working days each month.

traps: Grid and cluster are not the same. Both spread one job over many machines, but a cluster has one owner, one LAN and similar nodes, while a grid crosses organisations and needs middleware to negotiate access.
Utility computing is a billing model, not a cloud. Metered pricing without self-service and elasticity is just a hosting contract with an itemised bill.
Middleware is not the operating system. The OS runs one machine; middleware negotiates access across machines that each keep their own OS and their own rules.
In the worked example, do not charge all 300 servers for the month. Only the 5 peak days carry 300; the other 20 working days carry 20.
Homogeneous means same kind of hardware, not same job. The head node of a cluster is still homogeneous with its workers, yet it schedules while they compute.

quiz.a: A group of similar computers in one location, joined by a fast local network, owned and managed by one organisation, presented to users as one system.
Computing sold by the meter: the user pays per unit of use — server-hours, gigabytes stored, gigabytes transferred — instead of buying the machine.

quiz.q: Why does a grid need middleware while a cluster does not?
quiz.a: A cluster has one owner and administrator, so file systems, logins and scheduling are set up once for the group. A grid spans organisations that keep their own machines, operating systems and access rules, so middleware must authenticate the user, discover permitted resources and hide the differences.

quiz.q: What is a virtual organisation in grid computing?
quiz.a: A set of users from several institutions who are granted access to a shared pool of resources by agreement. Membership is defined by the agreement, not by which institution employs the user.

quiz.q: A site needs 100 servers for 4 working days each month and 10 servers for the other 16 working days. Renting costs ₹25 per server-hour, charged only for servers that are on. Find the monthly renting cost.
quiz.a: Peak hours = 100 × 4 × 24 = 9,600 server-hours. Off-peak hours = 10 × 16 × 24 = 3,840 server-hours. Total = 13,440 server-hours. Cost = 13,440 × ₹25 = ₹3,36,000 per month.

quiz.q: A vendor advertises metered billing and calls itself a cloud. Which two properties must you check before agreeing?
quiz.a: Self-service — can capacity be ordered through a console without human contact — and elasticity — does capacity grow and shrink automatically with load. Without both, metered billing is only utility computing or plain hosting.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a grid job usually delivers fewer useful CPU-hours per day than the same job on a cluster.
quiz.a: First, the wide area network between sites is slower than a LAN, so data transfer and synchronisation waste time. Second, heterogeneous machines and differing local policies mean the broker may place work on a slower or partly loaded machine, and trust and security overheads add further delay.

beyond: Not for the exam. The line did not stop at the cloud. Serverless computing (functions as a service) pushes utility billing down to a single request, so the meter ticks per invocation rather than per server-hour. Market-oriented clouds, covered in Unit 4, let buyers bid for spare capacity, the electricity market idea taken literally. On the operations side, cluster schedulers such as Slurm and container orchestrators in the Kubernetes style descend directly from the head node above. Search next for grid middleware, virtual organisation grid computing, and serverless billing models.
